blocks.text: 1. Planning

blocks.alt: A goal breaks into step 1, step 2, and step 3

blocks.text: Tool Calling established the basic request and execute mechanism every other capability in this module builds on. Planning, sequencing multiple tool calls toward a goal before acting, is the first of those capabilities, letting an agent handle goals a single tool call cannot answer.
It breaks a complex request into an ordered list of steps before executing any of them.
2. One Tool Call Versus A Sequence Of Calls

blocks.alt: One tool call is compared against a sequence of calls

blocks.text: A single tool call answers a query needing exactly one lookup.
A goal needing several ordered lookups requires planning that sequence first.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Goal type","What is needed"],"rows":[["Single lookup","One direct tool call"],["Several ordered, dependent lookups","A plan sequencing multiple tool calls"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Decomposing The Goal Into Steps

blocks.alt: A goal decomposes into step A and step B

blocks.text: As with multi-hop questions benefit most in Chain Of Thought, the agent breaks a broad goal into smaller, ordered sub-tasks.
Each sub-task mapped to a specific tool call to make.
4. Ordering Matters When Steps Depend On Each Other

blocks.alt: Step A leads to step B, which depends on A

blocks.text: As with hop two uses the first hop's result in Multi-Hop RAG, a later step often needs the output of an earlier step as its input.
The plan's step order is not arbitrary.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A plan step that looks up a customer's order ID before a later step checks that order's shipping status cannot run in reverse order, since the second step needs the first step's output.

blocks.text: 5. Planning Before Acting Versus Acting As You Go

blocks.alt: Planning first, then acting is compared against acting as you go

blocks.text: Committing to a full plan upfront differs from deciding the very next action one step at a time.
Both are valid agentic strategies with different tradeoffs.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Strategy","When the next step is decided"],"rows":[["Plan before acting","All steps decided upfront, before any execution"],["Act as you go","Each step decided based on the previous result"]]}

blocks.text: 6. Plans Need To Adapt To New Information

blocks.alt: An initial plan meets new information to produce a revised plan

blocks.text: As with the agent decides when enough information exists in Agentic RAG, an early step's actual result can invalidate a later step in the original plan.
A rigid plan that never revises itself risks following a now-wrong path.
7. Planning Adds Upfront Latency
As with each added step costs latency in Advanced RAG, producing a full plan before any tool call runs delays the first real action.
A real tradeoff against jumping straight into acting.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Generating a full multi-step plan before making even the first tool call adds real upfront latency, a cost worth weighing against the benefit of a well-ordered sequence.

blocks.text: 8. Planning Versus Reflection
Planning decides the steps before acting, while reflection, covered next in this module, evaluates the results after acting.
Two complementary halves of a full agentic loop.
9. Recognizing When Planning Earns Its Upfront Latency

blocks.alt: A goal needing multiple dependent steps points toward planning

blocks.text: Goals needing several ordered, dependent steps benefit from planning first.
A goal answerable with one direct tool call does not need a planning step at all.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Executing plan steps out of order when a later step depends on an earlier step's result.
Committing to a rigid plan that never revises itself when new information invalidates a step.
Adding a planning step for a goal answerable with a single direct tool call.
Forgetting that generating a full plan upfront adds real latency before the first action.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Planning sequences multiple tool calls toward a goal before executing any of them.
A single tool call suffices for one lookup; a multi-step goal requires planning the sequence.
The agent decomposes a broad goal into smaller, ordered sub-tasks mapped to tool calls.
Later steps often depend on earlier steps' results, so step order is not arbitrary.
Planning before acting and acting one step at a time are both valid, different strategies.
A plan must be able to adapt when an early step's actual result invalidates a later step.
Producing a full plan before any tool call runs adds real upfront latency.
Planning decides the steps before acting; reflection, covered next, evaluates results after acting.
Next up: Reflection, covering how an agent evaluates its own results after acting.
